faqs.a: We scope it structure by structure. faqs.q: Pigeons and starlings are nesting in our Stuarts Draft warehouse vents — is that covered?
faqs.a: Those two species, along with house sparrows, are the birds Virginia designates as nuisance species, so vent, dock, and sign-structure nesting can be handled directly: birds out, droppings cleaned, and vent and ledge hardware fitted so the flock cannot re-nest. Native birds are a different story — a chimney swift or barn swallow nest with eggs or young stays untouched until the young have left, and the exclusion hardware goes on after.

Stuarts Draft.wildlife_intro:
Stuarts Draft is the Valley's working landscape — South River farmland on one side of the road, distribution warehouses and food plants on the other — and each side generates its own calls. Farmhouses and ranch homes ringed by pasture get groundhogs under outbuildings and skunks under stoops, while the big commercial roofs collect pigeons and starlings at vents and dock doors, and Norway rats work grain, feed, and refuse areas. Big brown bats split the difference, roosting in older farmhouse attics all along the river bottom.

What ties a Stuarts Draft job together is scale. A groundhog system under a farm outbuilding, a bat colony above a farmhouse bedroom, and a starling problem at a dock are different crafts sharing one crew visit only if the inspection covers the whole property first. We map every structure, handle each species under its own Virginia rules, and seal in an order that keeps animals from simply moving from the barn to the house.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Weyers Cave attic?
faqs.a: Bats in Virginia are handled by exclusion only — one-way exits fitted and every other opening sealed so the colony leaves on its own. Under our permit conditions the maternity season runs May 1 through August 15, and bats may not be excluded or removed then unless no young are present or there is a threat to human health or safety, so we inspect any time but schedule most Weyers Cave exclusions outside that window. Since January 1, 2025, bat work also requires a CNAP holder with DWR-recognized bat training, which is how our crew works.

faqs.q: What should I expect to pay to sort out a snake at my Craigsville home?
faqs.a: Snake calls are priced around identification and access, not removal volume. A garter snake in a garden bed may need nothing but confirmation and habitat advice, while a rat snake inside a stone foundation takes careful extraction work. We inspect, tell you plainly which species you have and whether any action is warranted at all, and quote that specific work — honest snake jobs here sometimes end with advice and no chargeable removal, because most Craigsville snakes should simply be left alone.

faqs.q: I found a rattlesnake on the ridge behind my Craigsville house — what happens now?
faqs.a: Keep people and pets well back and do not try to move it. Timber rattlesnakes belong to these western ridges and rocky slopes, they are protected nongame wildlife in Virginia, and a snake on open ground away from the house usually moves off on its own. If one takes up residence in a woodpile, stone wall, or foundation where it cannot be avoided, call us: a permit holder can capture a non-listed snake and move it a short distance to suitable habitat within the same or a neighboring county, with the release-site landowner's written permission, and report it to DWR. Killing it is never the service.

Craigsville.wildlife_intro:
At Augusta County's western edge, Craigsville presses right against the mountains — the Little Calfpasture River runs through town and national forest ridges start where the yards end. That closeness shows in the work: black rat snakes and eastern garter snakes turn up in stone foundations and woodpiles, timber rattlesnakes live on the rocky ridges above town and are strictly a look-don't-touch safety call, and raccoons treat the town's older chimneys as ready-made den trees. On the ground, striped skunks dig under the close-built porches all winter long.

Mountain-edge jobs in Craigsville are identification jobs first. Most snakes here are harmless and protected as nongame wildlife, a spotted skunk — a declining western Virginia species — is a leave-alone call to the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources rather than a removal, and even the routine raccoon work follows Virginia's rule against moving animals off the property. We sort out what is actually at your foundation or in your flue before anything is trapped or sealed.
